sources.title: CLI Coding Agent (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: Points Claude Code, OpenCode, and Codex CLI at a local Qwen3.6 model served via Ollama's native 'launch' integration on DGX Spark, with no env vars or config files required.

facts.claim: OS/versions: Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS (DGX OS 7.3.1 base); Ollama v0.15+ required for `ollama launch`; last updated 04/16/2026.
Model variants: qwen3.6:latest (~24GB, 256K context), qwen3.6:35b-a3b-nvfp4 (~22GB, NVFP4), qwen3.6:35b-a3b-q8_0 (~39GB), qwen3.6:35b-a3b-bf16 (~71GB full precision).
Install: `curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh` then `ollama pull qwen3.6`.
Claude Code launch: `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash` then `ollama launch claude --model qwen3.6`.
OpenCode launch: `ollama launch opencode --model qwen3.6`. Codex CLI launch: `npm install -g @openai/codex` then `ollama launch codex --model qwen3.6`.

Playbook states: 'Use Ollama's built-in launch method to start [agent] against your local model. No environment variables or config files are required.' Setup takes 15-25 minutes; rollback = stop Ollama and delete ~/.ollama/models.

sources.relevance_to_us: Direct answer for 'how does Claude Code point at a local model on Spark' (ch15/ch16/ch17) — `ollama launch claude --model qwen3.6` is the exact wiring, zero config files. Confirms Steven's existing vLLM Qwen2.5-3B setup on WindowsDesktop is a different (manual endpoint) pattern vs. this Ollama-native one; worth comparing for the guide's local-agent chapter.

sources.title: Run Hermes Agent with Local Models (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: Deploys the always-on Hermes Agent TUI against a local vLLM-served Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 model, with an optional Telegram gateway that runs as a systemd service.

facts.claim: Install: `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/main/scripts/install.sh | bash`.
Model: nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4, served by vLLM as an OpenAI-compatible API on http://localhost:8000/v1 (port 8000).

Setup: launch vLLM serving Qwen3.6, run installer selecting 'Blank Slate', point installer at http://localhost:8000/v1, configure Telegram via `hermes gateway setup`, verify with `hermes` TUI command.
Quoted: 'The gateway runs as a system service, so the agent stays reachable across reboots without anyone logging in.'
Documentation verified against Hermes Agent v0.18.0 (2026.7.1); last updated 2026-06-12.

sources.relevance_to_us: Same vLLM/OpenAI-endpoint pattern (localhost:8000/v1) Steven already runs on WindowsDesktop for Qwen2.5-3B — this shows the Spark-native equivalent scaled to a 35B NVFP4 model, plus a systemd-service always-on agent pattern useful for ch16 (agentic validation loops).

sources.title: Run NemoClaw with a Local LLM (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: NemoClaw is NVIDIA's reference stack for running OpenClaw always-on assistants more safely, wrapping OpenClaw in the OpenShell sandbox with local vLLM inference, installed via a single curl-bash script.

facts.claim: Quoted definition: 'NVIDIA NemoClaw' is 'an open-source reference stack that simplifies running OpenClaw always-on assistants more safely,' integrating OpenShell runtime for security with local vLLM inference.
Install command: `curl -fsSL https://www.nvidia.com/nemoclaw.sh | bash`.
Default model: qwen3.6-35b-a3b-nvfp4, local vLLM inference on DGX Spark; web UI port auto-assigned (commonly 18789 or 18790).
Prereqs: DGX Spark (GB10) hardware, latest DGX OS, Ubuntu 24.04+, Docker 28.x+, Node.js 22.16+ (auto-installed if missing).
Key commands: `nemoclaw onboard` (custom setup), `nemoclaw my-assistant dashboard-url --quiet`, `nemoclaw my-assistant connect`, `nemoclaw my-assistant status`, `nemoclaw uninstall --yes`.
Full install ~30-60 minutes including model download.

sources.relevance_to_us: NemoClaw = the productized 'agent sandbox + always-on assistant' pattern for ch16 (local agentic validation loops); its single-command install and CLI surface (`nemoclaw <name> status/connect/dashboard-url`) is a clean model for a Spark-hosted Claude-adjacent validation agent.

sources.title: Set Up Example NemoClaw Agents (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: Four ready-to-run NemoClaw sample applications (news digest, dev agent, deck reviewer, calendar negotiator), all running inside OpenShell sandboxes with policy-based egress control and Nemotron 3 Super 120B via Ollama.

facts.claim: Four applications: Daily Personal News Digest (Telegram delivery), Software Development Agent (reads project dir, plans/implements/self-reviews/reports), Deck Reviewer (red-teams docs for consistency/sourcing/accessibility), Calendar Negotiator (meeting negotiation respecting focus blocks/timezones).
Model: Nemotron 3 Super 120B via Ollama (configurable); inference endpoint `inference.local` or a cloud provider.
Commands: `nemoclaw list`, `nemoclaw $SANDBOX_NAME status`, `nemoclaw $SANDBOX_NAME policy-add --from-file ./preset.yaml --yes`, `openshell policy get $SANDBOX_NAME --full`.
File transfer into sandbox: `tar czf - -C ~/source . | nemoclaw $SANDBOX_NAME exec -- bash -lc 'mkdir -p /sandbox/path && tar xzf - -C /sandbox/path'`.

Policy changes hot-reload without rebuild; filesystem policy changes require rebuild. Network egress requires explicit allowlists — default is blocked. Local model scheduling has DNS resolution limitations; cloud models work without workaround.

sources.relevance_to_us: The 'Software Development Agent' sample (plan→implement→self-review→report inside a sandbox) is nearly a template for ch16's local agentic validation loop; the default-deny egress + explicit allowlist policy model is directly reusable guidance for a Spark-hosted Claude Code sandbox.

sources.title: OpenClaw (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: OpenClaw is a local-first, privacy-preserving always-on AI agent for DGX Spark, configured to point at a local vLLM-served Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 endpoint with a 262,144-token context window.

facts.claim: Quoted: OpenClaw is 'a local-first AI agent that runs on your machine' combining memory, adaptation, continuous operation, and file/app context access, emphasizing on-device privacy.
Install: `curl -fsSL https://openclaw.ai/install.sh | bash`.
vLLM must be launched separately (following the vLLM playbook, Qwen3.6 agent-ready model), verified via `curl http://localhost:8000/v1/models`.
Configuration file: `nano ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json`. Model: nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4; endpoint http://localhost:8000/v1 (OpenAI-compatible); context window 262,144 tokens.

OpenClaw supports 'terminal access' and 'file system access' skills for developer workflows (install assistance, debugging), which the doc flags as carrying elevated security risk requiring careful skill management.

sources.relevance_to_us: Base layer that NemoClaw wraps with OpenShell sandboxing — useful to show the guide's readers the unsandboxed vs. sandboxed tradeoff explicitly (ch16, ch17 cost/blast-radius control).

sources.title: Secure Long Running AI Agents with OpenShell (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: OpenShell is NVIDIA's open-source sandbox runtime providing kernel-level isolation with declarative YAML policies for filesystem, network, and privilege control around long-running agents; wires a local vLLM inference provider and deploys OpenClaw inside a sandbox.

facts.claim: Quoted: OpenShell is 'an open-source sandbox runtime that wraps the agent in kernel-level isolation with declarative YAML policies,' with default-deny outbound network policy and real-time policy-decision monitoring.
Prereqs: DGX Spark 128GB unified memory, Ubuntu 24.04 (DGX OS), Docker Engine + NVIDIA Container Toolkit, Python 3.12+, `uv`, NVIDIA Sync configured, network access to PyPI and HuggingFace.

Install steps: `nvidia-smi`, `docker info`, `python3 --version` to verify; `sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker`; `curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/main/install.sh | sh`; serve model with vLLM on port 8000 with `--host 0.0.0.0`.

Provider setup: `openshell provider create --name local-vllm --type openai --credential OPENAI_API_KEY=not-needed --config OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://MACHINE_IP:8000/v1` then `openshell inference set --provider local-vllm --model nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4`.

Sandbox deploy: `openshell sandbox create --keep --tty --forward 18789 --name dgx-demo --from openclaw -- openclaw-start`. OpenShell v0.0.37+ manages the gateway as a systemd user service. Playbook serves the 35B model at 0.4 GPU memory utilization. Last updated 06/12/2026.

Doc quote: 'no system is perfect' — recommends isolation (clean VM), test accounts, vetting community skills, network restrictions, and credential cleanup as layered controls rather than perfect risk elimination.

sources.relevance_to_us: This is the concrete 'agent sandbox' answer for ch16 — kernel isolation + YAML policy + OpenAI-compatible provider pointed at local vLLM is the exact pattern for a bounded local agentic validation loop that can safely run Claude Code style automation on Spark without host-level blast radius.

sources.title: Build and Deploy a Multi-Agent Chatbot (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: Docker-composed multi-agent chatbot on DGX Spark: a gpt-oss-120B supervisor coordinating a Deepseek-Coder:6.7B coding sub-agent and Qwen3-Embedding-4B retrieval, served via llama.cpp/TensorRT-LLM with MCP-based tool access.

facts.claim: Models: Supervisor gpt-oss-120B (~63GB), Coding Agent Deepseek-Coder:6.7B-Instruct (~7GB), Embedding Qwen3-Embedding-4B (~4GB); total disk ~74GB for downloads.

Architecture: llama.cpp servers + TensorRT-LLM servers for inference, GPU-accelerated document retrieval, MCP servers exposed as supervisor-agent tools, backend API on localhost:8000, frontend UI on localhost:3000.

Setup: `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER && newgrp docker`; clone `github.com/NVIDIA/dgx-spark-playbooks`; `cd nvidia/multi-agent-chatbot/assets`; `chmod +x model_download.sh && ./model_download.sh`; `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose-models.yml up -d --build`.

Cleanup: `docker compose ... down` then `docker volume rm "$(basename "$PWD")_postgres_data"` (uses Postgres). Memory usage ~120GB of 128GB available. Deploy 10-20 min; model downloads 30 min-2 hours. Last updated November 20, 2025.

sources.relevance_to_us: Shows a mixed llama.cpp+TensorRT-LLM multi-model serving pattern with MCP tool exposure and Postgres state — good ch11/ch21 demo reference for a Flink-Agents-adjacent or NiFi-fronted multi-agent build; the ~120GB of 128GB memory footprint is a concrete concurrency/capacity data point for ch6.

sources.title: RAG Application in AI Workbench (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: GUI-driven deployment of NVIDIA's pre-built agentic RAG example project via AI Workbench's 'Clone Project' flow, requiring an NVIDIA API key and a Tavily web-search API key; the playbook itself does not document the underlying vector DB/embedding/LLM stack.

facts.claim: Repository: https://github.com/NVIDIA/workbench-example-agentic-rag, cloned via the AI Workbench GUI 'Clone Project' button.
Requires two API keys: NVIDIA API key from https://org.ngc.nvidia.com/setup/api-keys (must have 'Public API Endpoints' permission) and a Tavily API key from https://tavily.com/.
Hardware target: NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GB10 Superchip System; interface is a Gradio web UI. Last updated 10/28/2025.

No specific vector DB, embedding model, or LLM version is documented in this README — the WebFetch summary explicitly notes the guide 'abstains from detailing underlying technologies' and containerization abstracts the stack from the user.

sources.relevance_to_us: Weak as a direct RAG-stack reference (component details opaque); flag for ch15 that the actual embedding/vector-db choices need to come from the linked workbench-example-agentic-rag repo itself, not this playbook page, if the guide wants exact versions.

sources.title: Text to Knowledge Graph on DGX Spark (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: Docker-Compose stack that converts unstructured documents into an interactive knowledge graph using local Ollama LLM inference (default Llama 3.1 8B), ArangoDB with BM25 search, and a Next.js/Three.js WebGPU 3D visualization frontend.

facts.claim: Setup: `git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/dgx-spark-playbooks`, `cd nvidia/txt2kg/assets`, `./start.sh`; access web UI at http://localhost:3001.

Stack: LLM inference via Ollama with GPU acceleration (default Llama 3.1 8B), graph database ArangoDB with BM25 search, Three.js WebGPU rendering for visualization, Next.js frontend, Docker Compose + NVIDIA Container Toolkit deployment.
Additional model pull: `docker exec ollama-compose ollama pull <model-name>`.
Ollama tuning env vars used: OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1, OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=30m, OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS=1, OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0.
Setup ~2-3 min, model download 5-10 min. Last updated January 8, 2025 (predates most other playbooks — verify against live repo before citing as current).

sources.relevance_to_us: ArangoDB + BM25 + local Ollama extraction is a concrete alternative knowledge-store pattern to Qdrant for a local knowledge base (ch15); the Ollama env-var tuning knobs (KEEP_ALIVE, MAX_LOADED_MODELS, KV_CACHE_TYPE) are directly reusable for any Spark Ollama deployment in the guide.

sources.title: Video Search and Summarization (VSS) (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: Deploys NVIDIA's Video Search and Summarization AI Blueprint on DGX Spark, pairing a local Cosmos Reason 2 8B vision-language model with a remote LLM endpoint (recommended nvidia-nemotron-nano-9b-v2) for video Q&A, summarization, and real-time alerts.

facts.claim: Prereqs: DGX OS 7.4.0+, driver 580.95.05+, CUDA 13.0, NGC API key, 10GB+ storage in /tmp/.
Models: local VLM Cosmos Reason 2 8B; remote LLM via build.nvidia.com or self-hosted, recommended nvidia/nvidia-nemotron-nano-9b-v2.
Repo: `git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA-AI-Blueprints/video-search-and-summarization.git`, `git checkout tags/v3.2.0`.

Launch: `export NGC_CLI_API_KEY='...'`, `export LLM_ENDPOINT_URL=https://your-llm-endpoint.com`, `deploy/docker/scripts/dev-profile.sh up -p base -H DGX-SPARK --use-remote-llm --llm nvidia/nvidia-nemotron-nano-9b-v2`; Agent UI at http://localhost:7777 or http://<SPARK_IP>:7777.
Setup 30-45 min; rollback via `deploy/docker/scripts/dev-profile.sh down`. Last updated 06/17/2026.

sources.relevance_to_us: Concrete VLM+RAG pipeline for edge-AI video use cases (ch13/ch21 demo material) — pairs a local vision model with a remote text LLM, a hybrid pattern worth contrasting with the guide's local-only inference chapters (ch4/ch5).

sources.title: Live VLM WebUI (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: pipx-installed real-time webcam-to-VLM streaming UI on DGX Spark, defaulting to Ollama-served gemma3:4b with GPU monitoring and customizable prompts.

facts.claim: Install: `curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh`, `ollama pull gemma3:4b`; then `sudo apt install -y pipx`, `pipx ensurepath`, `pipx install live-vlm-webui`, `live-vlm-webui`.
Access at https://<SPARK_IP>:8090. VLM backend endpoint (Ollama default): http://localhost:11434/v1; alternatives include NVIDIA API Catalog, OpenAI, or custom endpoints.
Model alternatives listed: gemma3:4b (default, lightweight), llama3.2-vision:11b, qwen2.5-vl:7b.
Time estimate 20-30 minutes; risk level Low; requires a webcam and 10GB+ storage.

sources.relevance_to_us: Lightweight edge-AI/VLM demo (ch13/ch21) usable as a quick sensor-tie-in for MicroFi/AMOLED-class devices feeding a Spark-hosted VLM over the LAN.

sources.title: Vibe Coding in VS Code (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: Configures DGX Spark to serve GPT-OSS 120B via Ollama over the network so a remote VS Code + Continue.dev install can use it as a coding assistant, including opening the Ollama systemd service and firewall port.

facts.claim: Install/serve: `curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh`, `ollama pull gpt-oss:120b`.
Remote access config: `sudo systemctl edit ollama` (to bind beyond localhost), `sudo systemctl daemon-reload`, `sudo systemctl restart ollama`, `sudo ufw allow 11434/tcp`.
Verify from client: `curl -v http://YOUR_SPARK_IP:11434/api/version`.
VS Code ARM64 install via downloaded .deb: `sudo dpkg -i DOWNLOADED_PACKAGE_NAME`. Tooling: Continue.dev VS Code extension points at the remote Ollama endpoint.
Last updated 10/21/2025; no specific software versions listed otherwise.

sources.relevance_to_us: Direct pattern for ch3/ch15: exposing Ollama on 0.0.0.0:11434 through ufw so other array devices (e.g. WindowsDesktop VS Code) can use Spark as a shared coding-model host — same firewall-rule consideration as the existing EFM/Kafka LAN port-forward practice.

sources.title: VS Code (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: Installs VS Code natively (ARM64 .deb) on DGX Spark for desktop development, or configures NVIDIA Sync + SSH key auth for remote VS Code access, including hosting a local LLM code assistant.

facts.claim: Desktop install: `wget https://code.visualstudio.com/sha/download?build=stable&os=linux-deb-arm64 -O vscode-arm64.deb`, `sudo dpkg -i vscode-arm64.deb`, `sudo apt-get install -f`, `code &`.
Remote setup: install NVIDIA Sync, configure SSH key auth, launch VS Code through the Sync app for automatic remote connection.

Coverage includes an 'LLM code assistant hosting option' alongside extension installation, git integration testing, and integrated terminal use. ARM64-only. Duration 5 minutes; last updated July 23, 2026.
Uninstall: `sudo apt-get remove code`, optionally delete `~/.config/Code` and `~/.vscode`.

sources.relevance_to_us: Baseline dev-environment setup for ch3/ch15 if the guide recommends developing directly on the Spark box (matching how other array devices are worked from directly) rather than purely remote.

sources.title: Set Up Local Network Access (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: Covers connecting a laptop to DGX Spark over the local network via NVIDIA Sync or manual SSH, including mDNS hostname resolution and port-forwarding for web apps like the DGX Dashboard.

facts.claim: NVIDIA Sync install (Debian/Ubuntu): add gpg key + apt repo `deb https://workbench.download.nvidia.com/stable/linux/debian default proprietary`, then `sudo apt install nvidia-sync`.
Manual connect: `ssh -V` to verify, `ping spark-abcd.local` to test mDNS, `ssh <USERNAME>@<SPARK_HOSTNAME>.local` for initial connection.
Port forwarding for web apps: `ssh -L 11000:localhost:11000 <USERNAME>@<SPARK_HOSTNAME>.local`; DGX Dashboard runs on localhost:11000.
Time estimate 5-10 minutes; risk 'Low — SSH setup involves credential configuration but no system-level changes to the DGX Spark device.'

sources.relevance_to_us: Day-1 LAN join pattern for ch3 — the .local mDNS hostname convention plus SSH port-forwarding for the Dashboard is the minimum-viable way to bring the Spark onto the home LAN before Tailscale.

sources.title: Set up Tailscale on Your Spark (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: Installs and authenticates Tailscale on DGX Spark for secure remote-access mesh networking, using the official Tailscale apt repo for Ubuntu noble, with matching client setup on other devices.

facts.claim: Prereqs: DGX OS with Ubuntu 20.04+, sudo privileges, internet on both Spark and client devices, an identity provider account (Google/GitHub/Microsoft) for auth. Time estimate 15-30 min initial, 5 min per additional device.
SSH server install if needed: `sudo apt install -y openssh-server`, `sudo systemctl enable ssh --now --no-pager`.

Tailscale install: add keyring `curl -fsSL https://pkgs.tailscale.com/stable/ubuntu/noble.noarmor.gpg | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/tailscale-archive-keyring.gpg`, add repo list `.../noble.tailscale-keyring.list`, `sudo apt install -y tailscale`.
Authenticate with `sudo tailscale up`. Client devices join with the same identity-provider account; Linux clients also run `sudo tailscale up`.
Rollback: 'Tailscale can be completely removed with `sudo apt remove tailscale`' and network routing automatically reverts to defaults.

sources.relevance_to_us: Directly maps to ch3's Tailscale plan for joining NvidiaSpark-1 to the array's mesh network — exact apt-repo/keyring commands for Ubuntu noble, ready to drop into the guide.

sources.title: DGX Dashboard (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: The DGX Dashboard is a web UI on port 11000 providing system update management, GPU/resource telemetry monitoring, and an integrated per-user JupyterLab environment on DGX Spark.

facts.claim: Quoted: dashboard provides 'a graphical interface for system updates, resource monitoring, and an integrated JupyterLab environment.'
Dashboard server port: 11000. JupyterLab uses per-user assigned ports stored in `/opt/nvidia/dgx-dashboard-service/jupyterlab_ports.yaml`.

Check JupyterLab port: `cat /opt/nvidia/dgx-dashboard-service/jupyterlab_ports.yaml`. Remote tunnel for both: `ssh -L 11000:localhost:11000 -L <ASSIGNED_PORT>:localhost:<ASSIGNED_PORT> <USERNAME>@<SPARK_DEVICE_IP>`.
No explicit DGX OS version number given in this README; last update November 21, 2025, described as minor copyedits only.

sources.relevance_to_us: Port 11000 dashboard + per-user JupyterLab is the ch14 observability starting point for Spark, and a natural companion to whatever prometheus exporters the guide adds for GPU telemetry.

sources.title: Register DGX Spark to Brev (DGX Spark Playbooks)
sources.summary: Registers DGX Spark as a managed compute node with NVIDIA Brev, enabling remote access, team GPU-environment sharing, and Launchable-based standardized environments; README omits the actual registration command.

facts.claim: Quoted: Brev 'makes GPU environments remotely accessible, shareable, and easy to standardize using preconfigured setups called Launchables.'
Deregister: `brev deregister`. Troubleshoot connectivity: `brev refresh`. Change org: `brev set <my-org>`.
Prereqs: NVIDIA Brev account created at login.brev.nvidia.com, DGX Spark already set up, admin/root or sudo access.

The extraction notes the README states registration is interactive ('In the CLI, you'll be walked through registration') but does not print the exact initial registration command; estimated time 5-10 minutes, risk level Low.

sources.relevance_to_us: Optional ch3/ch21 mention for remote-team GPU sharing via Brev Launchables — lower priority than Tailscale for a home-lab single-operator setup but worth a callout for the 'team access' angle.

open_questions: Which coding-agent launch pattern does the guide want to standardize on: Ollama-native `ollama launch claude --model ...` (cli-coding-agent) or manual OpenAI-compatible endpoint pointing (vLLM-based hermes-agent/openclaw/openshell pattern)? They imply different install footprints.

rag-ai-workbench's README does not document its actual vector DB/embedding/LLM stack — needs a follow-up fetch of https://github.com/NVIDIA/workbench-example-agentic-rag directly if ch15 wants exact RAG component versions.
txt2kg's README is dated January 8, 2025 — much older than the other playbooks (most 2025-11 through 2026-07) — worth verifying it hasn't been superseded or removed before citing as current guidance.

register-to-brev's README omits the actual initial `brev` registration command; if ch3/ch21 wants to show Brev onboarding end-to-end, that command needs sourcing from Brev's own docs, not this playbook.

load_bearing_claims.why_it_matters: This is the concrete 'agent sandbox' mechanism the guide's ch16 (local agentic validation loops) needs to describe safe, bounded automated-agent execution on the Spark box.
